title: sed basics
text:
On this page, you use sed to change text: you replace one piece of text with another, delete lines you do not need, and turn a file with another column separator into the tab-separated table. You will use these command to clean up a file that was saved on Windows and that contains a problem that can quietly break your AWK commands.
Why would you change text with a command, and not by hand? Two jobs come up again and again in biology:
sed does both jobs with one short command, and like AWK, it never changes the file it reads unless you ask for that. You use the same folder as on the last page, with the data in awk_data/.

title: sed basics
section: The shape of a sed command
text:
The shape of a sed command
The command you use most often in sed is s, for substitute (replace):
sed 's/old/new/' file

s tells sed to replace text.
old is the text to look for, and new the text to put in its place. The three slashes / separate the parts.
The part between single quotes is the sed command. Like in AWK, it always goes between single quotes.

sed reads the file one line at a time, makes the change on each line where it finds old, and prints every line, changed or not. For example, to shorten low_P to low:

sed 's/low_P/low/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low mock    ex61    38  6.8
The file itself is not changed. sed only printed a changed version on the screen:

head -3 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8

title: sed basics
section: The g flag: change every match in a line
text:
The g flag: change every match in a line
Say you want a comma-separated table instead of a tab-separated one. In sed, \t stands for a tab, so you replace \t with ,:

sed 's/\t/,/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient,Condition  Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P,mock  ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P,mock  ex61    38  6.8
We see that this command didn’t exactly do what we wanted and only the first tab of each line became a comma. That is because by default, s changes only the first match in a line. To change every match, add the flag g (for “global”) after the last slash. A flag is a letter that changes how a command works:

sed 's/\t/,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient,Condition,Experiment,Rootlength,FW_shoot_mg
low_P,mock,ex61,40.4,6.6
low_P,mock,ex61,38,6.8
To check that this worked on the whole file, not only the first lines, count the fields per line with AWK, as on the last page. Since this time the fields are separated by commas, you use -F',':

sed 's/\t/,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | awk -F',' '{ print NF }' | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
    595 5
All 595 lines have 5 fields, so every tab was replaced.






QuestionExercise






Replace mock with control, and look at the first 3 lines of the result.
How many lines contain control after the change (use grep for this task)? Afterwards, confirm the number with AWK: how many lines have mock in column 2 in the original file?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# 1. Replace and look
sed 's/mock/control/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

# 2. Count after the change, and check with awk on the original file
sed 's/mock/control/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c 'control'
awk -F'\t' '$2 == "mock"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   control ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   control ex61    38  6.8

209
209
Both give 209, so sed changed exactly the 209 mock plants. mock appears at most once per line, so you do not need the g flag here.

title: sed basics
text:
Special characters: the dot
The text you look for in sed is not plain text, but a regular expression: a pattern in which some characters have a special meaning. Most letters and numbers just mean themselves. But a dot . means “any one character”. See what happens when you try to replace the decimal points with commas:

sed 's/./,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -2

This prints:
,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,
,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,
We see that every character, letters and tabs included, became a comma. To look for a real dot, you need to put a backslash \ before it in order to take away the special meaning from .:

sed 's/\./,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40,4    6,6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6,8
You can do a quick sanity check: the number of lines with a comma after the change should equal the number of lines with a dot before. In grep, the dot is special too, so you need the backslash there as well:

sed 's/\./,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c ','
grep -c '\.' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
590
590
Other characters with a special meaning include *, [, ], ^ and $. You meet $ at the end of this page. If the text you want to replace contains one of them, put a backslash before it.

title: sed basics
section: sed sees the whole line, not columns
text:
sed sees the whole line, not columns
On the last page, grep '13' found 36 more lines than the plants with bacterium 13C, because 13 also appears in numbers such as 13.3. sed has the same problem: it looks for patterns in the whole line, not only in a single column. To test this, replace 13 with X, then count and look at the lines with an X:

sed 's/13/X/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c 'X'
sed 's/13/X/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep 'X' | head -3

This prints:
211

low_P   mock    ex61    55.3    X.3
low_P   mock    ex61    48.7    X.9
low_P   mock    ex64    46.93   X.52
211 lines changed, but only 175 plants have bacterium 13C. The first lines with an X are not even 13C plants: they are mock plants whose shoot weight 13.3 became X.3, without any warning. Two ways to avoid this:

Make the text you look for more specific: 13C appears only in column 2.
If the change must happen in one column only, use AWK, which can compare and change a single field.


# More specific text
sed 's/13C/strain13C/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c 'strain13C'

# Only column 2, with AWK
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$2 == "13C" { $2 = "strain13C" } { print }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c 'strain13C'

This prints:
175
175
Both change exactly the 175 lines of the 13C plants.

title: sed basics
text:
Several changes in one command
To make more than one change, separate the s commands with a semicolon ;. sed runs them one after the other, on each line:

sed 's/low_P/low/; s/high_P/high/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
      1 Nutrient
    294 high
    300 low

A file with another column separator
Not every table separates its columns with tabs. The file Growth_Data_dutch.csv holds the same growth data, but with semicolons between the columns and commas as decimal symbol. You may get files like this from a spreadsheet program. Look at it first, as always:

head -3 awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | cat -A

This prints:
Nutrient;Condition;Experiment;Rootlength;FW_shoot_mg$
low_P;mock;ex61;40,4;6,6$
low_P;mock;ex61;38;6,8$
There is no ^I, so there are no tabs. A file ending in .csv (“comma-separated values”) does not always use commas: always check which character separates the columns before you use the file. Here it is ;, so in AWK you would use -F';':

awk -F';' '{ print NF }' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
    595 5
To turn this file into a tab-separated table with decimal points, you need two changes: commas to dots, and semicolons to tabs.
In the code below, you may wonder why s/,/./g needs no backslash before the dot. The dot is special only in the part you look for, the old part. In the new part, it is just a dot. Here you look for a comma, which has no special meaning, and put a dot in its place.
Save the result in a new file, and check it:

sed 's/,/./g; s/;/\t/g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv > Growth_Data_from_csv.txt

# Check: look at it, count the lines and the fields per line
head -3 Growth_Data_from_csv.txt
wc -l Growth_Data_from_csv.txt
awk -F'\t' '{ print NF }' Growth_Data_from_csv.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8

595 Growth_Data_from_csv.txt

    595 5
In this tutorial, you can even check that the result is exactly the original table. cmp compares two files byte by byte. It prints nothing if they are identical, so && echo 'identical' prints a message in that case:

cmp Growth_Data_from_csv.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt && echo 'identical'

This prints:
identical






QuestionExercise






Turn Growth_Data_dutch.csv into a real comma-separated file: commas between the columns, and dots as decimal symbol. Check the result with head and with the number of fields per line.
Now swap the order of the two changes in your command. What happens, and why?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# 1. First the decimal commas to dots, then the semicolons to commas
sed 's/,/./g; s/;/,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | head -3
sed 's/,/./g; s/;/,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | awk -F',' '{ print NF }' | sort | uniq -c

# 2. The other order
sed 's/;/,/g; s/,/./g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | head -3
sed 's/;/,/g; s/,/./g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | awk -F',' '{ print NF }' | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
Nutrient,Condition,Experiment,Rootlength,FW_shoot_mg
low_P,mock,ex61,40.4,6.6
low_P,mock,ex61,38,6.8
    595 5

Nutrient.Condition.Experiment.Rootlength.FW_shoot_mg
low_P.mock.ex61.40.4.6.6
low_P.mock.ex61.38.6.8
    595 1
In the second command, sed first turns the semicolons into commas. The second change then turns all commas into dots, the new column separators included. Each line is now one single field. sed runs the changes in the order you write them, and each change works on the result of the one before.

title: sed basics
text:
Delete lines
Besides s, sed has a command d to delete lines. In front of d, you say which lines: a line number, or a pattern between slashes. To delete the header, line 1:

sed '1d' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -2
sed '1d' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8

594
To delete every line that contains high_P we can do the following (and also compare with AWK):

sed '/high_P/d' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$1 != "high_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
301
301
301 lines: the header and the 300 low_P plants. As with s, sed looks for the pattern in the whole line. Here that is fine, because high_P appears only in column 1.






TipTip: print only some lines with -n and p (optional)





sed prints every line by default. With -n, it prints nothing, unless you ask for it with the command p (print). This is a quick way to look at one line, or a range of lines, by number:

# Line 123, the first plant without a root length
sed -n '123p' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Lines 2 to 4
sed -n '2,4p' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
high_P  mock    ex61        18.2
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8
low_P   mock    ex61    74.7    8.1
awk 'NR == 123' from the last page does the same.









QuestionExercise






Delete the header and all plants from experiment ex65, with one sed command. How many lines are left? Check the number with AWK.







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Two commands, separated by ;
sed '1d; /ex65/d' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

# Check: rows after the header, where column 3 is not ex65
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $3 != "ex65"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
399
399

title: sed basics
text:
Change a file safely
So far, sed only printed its result, or you saved it in a new file. Sometimes you want to change a file itself, for example to correct a name in a table you keep using. Do this on a copy, never on your original data.
For the rest of this page, you use a second table, mmc5_metadata.txt. It describes 27 bacterial strains, for example their taxonomy and the plant they were isolated from. It comes from a published study, and two of its strains are the bacteria 129E and 13C from the growth data. On the next page, you combine the two tables.
Make a copy, so the file in awk_data/ stays as it is, and look at the strains isolated from legumes. The table has 12 columns, so cut -f1,6 shows only the strain name (column 1) and the host plant (column 6):

cp awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt metadata.txt
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt | cut -f1,6

This prints:
USDA61  Legume
R7A Legume
CIAT899 Legume
NGR234  Legume
C58 Legume
The safe way to change a file has three steps: write the result to a new file, check it, and only then replace the old file with the new one. Say you want Legume_host instead of Legume:

# 1. Write the result to a new file
sed 's/Legume/Legume_host/' metadata.txt > metadata_new.txt

# 2. Check: the same number of lines, and only the lines you wanted changed
wc -l metadata.txt metadata_new.txt
diff metadata.txt metadata_new.txt | cut -f1,6

This prints:
  28 metadata.txt
  28 metadata_new.txt
  56 total

4c4
< USDA61    Legume
---
> USDA61    Legume_host
7c7
< R7A   Legume
---
> R7A   Legume_host
10c10
< CIAT899   Legume
---
> CIAT899   Legume_host
17c17
< NGR234    Legume
---
> NGR234    Legume_host
20c20
< C58   Legume
---
> C58   Legume_host
diff compares two files line by line and prints only the lines that differ. 4c4 means: line 4 was changed. Lines starting with < come from the first file, lines starting with > from the second. diff prints whole lines, which are long in this table, so | cut -f1,6 keeps only the strain and the host. Lines such as 4c4 have no tab, and cut prints them as they are. So exactly five lines changed, the way you wanted. Now replace the old file:

# 3. Replace the old file with the new one
mv metadata_new.txt metadata.txt
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt | cut -f1,6

This prints:
USDA61  Legume_host
R7A Legume_host
CIAT899 Legume_host
NGR234  Legume_host
C58 Legume_host

sed -i: change the file itself
sed can also change a file directly, with the option -i (for “in place”). It does the three steps above in one go, but without the check. This is often were mistakes happen. Say you forgot that you already made the change, and run the command again, this time with -i:

sed -i 's/Legume/Legume_host/' metadata.txt
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt | cut -f1,6

This prints:
USDA61  Legume_host_host
R7A Legume_host_host
CIAT899 Legume_host_host
NGR234  Legume_host_host
C58 Legume_host_host
Legume_host still contains Legume, so sed added _host a second time. sed gives no warning, and the old version of the file is gone. This happens easily when you run a script or a notebook a second time.
If you use -i, let sed keep a backup copy. With -i.bak, sed saves the old version as metadata.txt.bak before it changes the file:

sed -i.bak 's/Legume_host_host/Legume_host/' metadata.txt
ls metadata*
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt | cut -f1,6
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt.bak | cut -f1,6

This prints:
metadata.txt
metadata.txt.bak

USDA61  Legume_host
R7A Legume_host
CIAT899 Legume_host
NGR234  Legume_host
C58 Legume_host

USDA61  Legume_host_host
R7A Legume_host_host
CIAT899 Legume_host_host
NGR234  Legume_host_host
C58 Legume_host_host






ImportantBefore you use sed -i




Work on a copy, not on your original data.
If you are not sure, write to a new file first and check it with wc -l and diff.
Ask yourself what happens if the command runs twice. A change like s/Legume/Legume_host/ grows each time, s/Legume_host_host/Legume_host/ does not.









QuestionExercise






Add _host to every host in column 6 of awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt, and save the result in a new file. First look at which hosts there are. Do it once with sed, and once with AWK. Tip: on the AWK page, you glued text together with $1"-"$2.
Check both results: count the values in column 6, and compare the two files.







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Which hosts are there?
cut -f6 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | sort | uniq -c

# 1a. sed: one change per host
sed 's/Legume/Legume_host/; s/Arabidopsis/Arabidopsis_host/' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > hosts_sed.txt

# 1b. AWK: glue _host to column 6, on every line after the header
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 { $6 = $6 "_host" } { print }' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > hosts_awk.txt

# 2. Check
cut -f6 hosts_sed.txt | sort | uniq -c
cut -f6 hosts_awk.txt | sort | uniq -c
cmp hosts_sed.txt hosts_awk.txt && echo 'identical'

This prints:
     22 Arabidopsis
      5 Legume
      1 host

     22 Arabidopsis_host
      5 Legume_host
      1 host

     22 Arabidopsis_host
      5 Legume_host
      1 host

identical
Both commands give the same file, and most strains turn out to come from Arabidopsis, like the plants in the growth data. The sed version works here because you looked first: there are only two hosts, and these two words appear nowhere else in the table. With many different hosts, you would need one change for each.
The AWK version changes column 6 on every line, whatever is in it. $6 "_host" glues the text _host to the value in column 6. Three mistakes give a wrong result without an error:

Without NR > 1, the header becomes host_host.
Run the command a second time, on hosts_awk.txt, and you get Arabidopsis_host_host, as with sed -i above.
Without the double quotes around _host, AWK reads _host as the name of an empty variable, and nothing changes.













TipTip: sed on a Mac (optional)






The sed on a Mac is a different version (BSD sed). Two differences matter for this page: sed -i needs a backup ending after it (sed -i '' ... for no backup, or sed -i.bak ...), and \t may not mean a tab in the text you look for. If a command from this page does not work on your Mac, this is a likely reason.

title: sed basics
text:
Windows line endings
Every line in a text file ends with an invisible character that says “a new line starts here”. Linux and Mac use one character for this, written as \n. Windows uses two: \r\n. A table saved on Windows, for example from Excel, may therefore have a hidden \r at the end of every line. You do not see it on screen, but AWK and grep on Linux see it as part of the last column.
The metadata table was saved from Excel on Windows. file tells you what kind of text a file holds. Compare it with the growth data:

file awk_data/Growth_Data.txt awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt

This prints:
awk_data/Growth_Data.txt:   ASCII text
awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt: ASCII text, with CRLF line terminators
CRLF is the name for the Windows line ending \r\n. Now see what it does. Column 12, the last column, holds TRUE, FALSE or NA. Count these values with the tools from the CLI workshop, and then let AWK count the rows with TRUE:

cut -f12 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | sort | uniq -c
awk -F'\t' '$12 == "TRUE"' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | wc -l

This prints:
      1 Colonization
      3 FALSE
     13 NA
     11 TRUE

0
cut shows 11 rows with TRUE, but AWK finds 0, and there is no error. That happens because column 12 is TRUE\r, not TRUE. The \r is invisible on screen, also in the output of cut above. cat -A shows it as ^M. Column 12 is the last column, so cut -f1,12 gives a short view of the strain name and the line end:

head -3 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | cut -f1,12
head -3 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | cut -f1,12 | cat -A

This prints:
strain  Colonization
Root123D2   NA
Root381 NA

strain^IColonization^M$
Root123D2^INA^M$
Root381^INA^M$

Remove the \r with sed
To remove the \r, replace it with nothing. In sed, \r stands for this character, and $ means “the end of the line”. So s/\r$// removes a \r only where it sits at the end of a line:

sed 's/\r$//' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt

# Check: file type, the hidden characters, the number of lines and characters,
# and the count from before
file mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
head -3 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | cut -f1,12 | cat -A
wc -l mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
wc -c awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
awk -F'\t' '$12 == "TRUE"' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | wc -l

This prints:
mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt: ASCII text

strain^IColonization$
Root123D2^INA$
Root381^INA$

28 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt

2808 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt
2780 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
5588 total

11
The ^M is gone, and AWK finds the 11 rows. wc -c counts characters: the fixed file has 28 lines and 28 characters fewer, one \r per line. Keep mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt, you use it on the next page.






ImportantGit Bash hides this problem



The outputs on this page come from Linux (Ubuntu in WSL). In Git Bash on Windows, AWK and grep ignore the \r: they find 11 rows with TRUE also in the original file. The file still has the \r, though, and file, cat -A and sed show it in Git Bash too. As soon as you use the file on Linux, for example on a computer cluster, the problem appears. So check new files with file or cat -A, whatever system you work on.








TipTip: remove the \r with tr (optional)





You will often see another command for the same job: tr -d '\r' deletes every \r in a file. tr reads only from a pipe or with <, not from a file name:

tr -d '\r' < awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > mmc5_metadata_fixed_tr.txt
cmp mmc5_metadata_fixed_tr.txt mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt && echo 'identical'

This prints:
identical
Both commands give the same result here.

title: sed basics
text:
What you learned

sed 's/old/new/' file replaces the first match in each line, s/old/new/g every match.
The text you look for is a regular expression: . means any character, \. a real dot. \t is a tab, \r the hidden Windows character, $ the end of a line.
sed looks at the whole line, not at columns. Make the text you look for specific, or use AWK to change one column.
Separate several changes with ;. They run in the order you write them.
sed '1d' deletes line 1, sed '/text/d' every line that contains text.
Check which character separates the columns before you use a file, also when it ends in .csv.
Change a file safely: work on a copy, write to a new file, check with wc -l and diff, then replace. With sed -i, keep a backup (-i.bak), and think about what happens if the command runs twice.
Windows line endings (\r, ^M in cat -A) make text matches on the last column fail without an error. Find them with file or cat -A, and remove them with sed 's/\r$//'.

On the next page, Combining two files, you add information from the strain metadata to the growth data.

title: Welcome
text:
This tutorial shows you how to work with tables and other text files on the command line with two small tools: AWK and sed. You use them to select rows and columns, to calculate sums and means, to clean up names, and to combine information from two files. You will try every command on real biological data, a table with plant growth measurements and a set of 16S sequences.
Important: This tutorial is still work in progress, missing chapters will be added over time

title: Welcome
text:
What are AWK and sed?
AWK is a small programming language made for tables. It reads a file one line at a time and splits each line into fields, the separate values in a line, like the cells in one row of a spreadsheet. You then tell AWK what to do with these fields, for example “print the second and fourth column” or “keep only the rows where the root length is above 50”.
sed (short for “stream editor”) reads a file one line at a time and changes the text on the fly. You use it mostly to search and replace, for example to shorten a long sequence name, or to delete lines you do not need.
Both tools come with almost every Linux and Mac system, they work on files of any size, and they need only one line of code for many everyday tasks. That is why you meet them in many bioinformatics scripts and tutorials.

title: Welcome
section: Why not just use Excel or R?
text:
Why not just use Excel or R?
For statistics and plots, R or Python are the better tools. But for many smaller jobs, AWK and sed have some real advantages:

You keep a record of what you did. A command can be saved in a script or a notebook, and run again on new data. A table that you change by hand in Excel leaves no record, and Excel sometimes changes your data without asking: it is known to turn gene names such as SEPT2 into dates.
The same step works on many files. Together with a for loop, one command can clean the names in 50 FASTA files, or take one column from 200 sample tables.
Nothing to install. AWK and sed are already on your computer and on most computer clusters, so you do not need packages or extra software.

title: Welcome
section: Why learn this when an LLM can write it?
text:
Why learn this when an LLM can write it?
LLMs (large language models, such as ChatGPT or Claude) are good at writing AWK and sed commands. So it is not the goal of this tutorial to make you write long AWK programs from memory. Instead, after this tutorial you should be able to:

read a short AWK or sed command, and say what it does
check whether it does what you asked for, on your own data
adapt it, for example to use another column or another file
recognize the common traps, where a command runs without an error but gives the wrong result

The last point matters most. A command that fails with an error message is easy to notice. A command that quietly skips a few rows, or treats a missing value as a zero, is not.

title: Welcome
text:
What you will do

Use AWK on a table: print and select columns and rows, add a column, and calculate counts and means per group
Learn sed basics: search and replace text, delete lines, and change a file safely
Use AWK and sed on FASTA files: count sequences, measure their lengths, clean up sequence names, and add information from a second file (in planning)
Checking code from an LLM: a short routine to test any AWK or sed command before you trust its output (in planning)

title: Welcome
text:
Before you start
To follow this tutorial you need:

A terminal and the command line basics. This tutorial assumes you have worked through the basics of the CLI workshop: moving around with cd and ls, looking at files with head and wc, and combining commands with a pipe (|). It also helps if you have used grep and cut. If you have never opened a terminal, start with Before you start of the CLI workshop.
Your own computer. All commands are meant to run on your laptop. If you already know how to use Crunchomics, the UvA computer cluster, you can also work there (see the HPC pages of the CLI workshop).
The example data. You download it at the start of the first page, with two commands. It is small (about 10 kB), so it fits on any laptop.







ImportantAWK and sed are not the same on every computer



There are several versions of AWK and sed. Linux systems and Crunchomics usually have the GNU versions, Macs have different (BSD) versions, and the terminal in MobaXterm may have yet another one. Most commands in this tutorial work everywhere, and where a command behaves differently, the page says so. 


Start with AWK on a table.

title: AWK on a table
text:
On this page, you use AWK on a real table with plant growth measurements. You choose columns, keep the rows you need, add a new column, and calculate means per group. Along the way, you meet the most common trap when you work with tables: missing values that quietly change your results.
The same commands work on any table in plain text, and many bioinformatics tools write their results that way, for example BLAST, featureCounts or a GFF annotation file. With AWK you can filter or reshape such output right away, or pass it on to the next tool with a pipe, without saving it first or opening it in R. AWK never changes the file it reads: it prints the result on the screen, or into a new file if you ask for that.
The outputs on these pages come from a Linux computer (Ubuntu in WSL). On most computers you get the same result. Where this is not the case, the page says so.

title: AWK on a table
section: Get the data: curl and tar
text:
Get the data: curl and tar
All example files for this tutorial come in one file, awk_data.tar.gz. A .tar.gz file packs many files into one and compresses them, similar to a .zip file.

# Go to your home folder, and make a folder for this tutorial
cd ~
mkdir awk_tutorial
cd awk_tutorial

# Download the data
# -L: if the link sends you on to another address, follow it
# -O: save the file under its own name, awk_data.tar.gz
curl -L -O "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/AWK_tutorial/main/data/awk_data.tar.gz"

# Unpack it. Used options:
# -x extract, -z it is compressed (.gz), -f the file name follows
tar -xzf awk_data.tar.gz

# Check: you should see awk_data and awk_data.tar.gz
ls

# Check: you should see 14 files
ls awk_data
ls awk_data | wc -l

On this page you only need Growth_Data.txt. The other files are 16S sequences, a table with information on bacterial strains, and a second version of the growth table, which you use on later pages.






WarningDraft note



The download link is not tested yet: the data is not on GitHub yet. The other commands were tested on a copy of the same file.

title: AWK on a table
text:
Look at the table first
Before you run any command on a table, you want to look at it first. You at leat want to know: how many lines it has, and what separates the columns?

# The first 5 lines
head -5 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# The number of lines
wc -l awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8
low_P   mock    ex61    74.7    8.1
low_P   mock    ex61    34.4    8.3

595 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt
We see that the table has a header, a first line with the column names, and 594 rows of measurements. Each row is one plant and we have the following columns:

Nutrient: the plant grew with low or high phosphorus (low_P, high_P)
Condition: the plant was inoculated with nothing (mock) or with one of two bacteria (129E, 13C)
Experiment: the experiment the plant was part of (ex61, ex64, ex65)
Rootlength: root length in mm
FW_shoot_mg: shoot fresh weight in mg

The columns look like they are separated by spaces. However, you cannot see what is really there, because spaces and tabs look the same on screen. cat -A shows the invisible characters:

head -3 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | cat -A

This prints:
Nutrient^ICondition^IExperiment^IRootlength^IFW_shoot_mg$
low_P^Imock^Iex61^I40.4^I6.6$
low_P^Imock^Iex61^I38^I6.8$
Here, ^I is a tab, and $ marks the end of each line. So this tells us that we work with a tab-separated table. You need to know this for the next steps.






TipTip: cat -A on a Mac (optional)






On a Mac, cat -A may not work. cat -et shows the same: tabs as ^I and line ends as $.

title: AWK on a table
section: The shape of an AWK command
text:
The shape of an AWK command
Every AWK command on this page has the same shape:
awk -F'\t' 'pattern { action }' file

-F'\t' tells AWK that the columns are separated by tabs. -F stands for field separator. A field is one value in a line, like one cell in a spreadsheet row.
'pattern { action }' is the AWK program, it always needs to be between single quotes. The pattern says which lines to work on. The action, between curly brackets, says what to do with them.
file is the file AWK reads.

AWK reads the file one line at a time. For each line, it checks the pattern. If the line matches, AWK runs the action. You can leave out either part: without a pattern, the action runs on every line. Without an action, AWK prints the lines that match.

title: AWK on a table
text:
print: choose columns
AWK gives each field of a line a number: $1 is the first field, $2 the second, and so on. $0 is the whole line. To print the first column:

# Print column 1 of every line, and show the first 3 lines of the result
awk -F'\t' '{ print $1 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient
low_P
low_P
To print several columns, separate the fields you want with a comma:

# Print column 1 (Nutrient) and column 4 (Rootlength)
awk -F'\t' '{ print $1, $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient Rootlength
low_P 40.4
low_P 38
AWK puts a space between the printed columns. To keep the result a tab-separated table, tell AWK to use a tab in the output too. -v OFS='\t' sets the output field separator:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '{ print $1, $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient    Rootlength
low_P   40.4
low_P   38
You can do the same thing with cut -f1,4 (something you might have seen in our CLI workshop). AWK becomes more useful in the next sections, where you choose rows too.
A quick check for any table is to count the fields in each line. NF is the number of fields in the current line:

# Count the fields per line, then count how often each number occurs
awk -F'\t' '{ print NF }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
    595 5
This tells us that all 595 lines have 5 fields. If some lines had 4 or 6, something in the table would be off and together this gives us a quick command to check that our data has the right structure.






QuestionExercise






Print the columns Experiment and FW_shoot_mg, separated by a tab. Look at the first 4 lines of the result.







AnswerClick me to see an answer





Experiment is column 3 and FW_shoot_mg is column 5:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '{ print $3, $5 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -4

This prints:
Experiment  FW_shoot_mg
ex61    6.6
ex61    6.8
ex61    8.1

title: AWK on a table
text:
NR: the header line
NR is the number of the record, the line AWK is reading now. You use it in a pattern to choose lines by their position:

# Only line 1, the header
awk -F'\t' 'NR == 1' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# All lines after the header: show the first 2, and count them
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -2
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8
594
These commands have only a pattern and no action, so AWK prints the lines that match. NR > 1 skips the header and keeps all 594 rows of data. You need it often, as the next sections show.

title: AWK on a table
text:
Subset rows by text
To keep only the rows of the plants grown with low phosphorus, compare column 1 with the text low_P:

awk -F'\t' '$1 == "low_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3
awk -F'\t' '$1 == "low_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8
low_P   mock    ex61    74.7    8.1

300
Two details matter here:

Text goes between double quotes: "low_P". Without quotes, AWK reads low_P as the name of a variable, a named box that holds a value. That box is empty, so no row matches.
To compare, use two equal signs: ==. If you would use only one equal sign this command would do something else and instead put a value into a field. Note here, how AWK gives you no error message and only by inspecting the output we will see that the command is doing something different to what we wanted:


# Wrong: one = instead of two
awk -F'\t' '$1 = "low_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3
awk -F'\t' '$1 = "low_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
low_P Condition Experiment Rootlength FW_shoot_mg
low_P mock ex61 40.4 6.6
low_P mock ex61 38 6.8

595
Here, every line is kept, but column 1 of every line now says low_P, even in the header, and the tabs became spaces. A quick wc -l shows the problem: 595 lines, the same as the whole file.

Why not use grep?
If you have followed the CLI workshop you might remember grep, which keeps lines that contain a word. For the plants with bacterium 13C, both tools give the same count:

grep '13C' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$2 == "13C"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
175
175
But there is an important difference: grep searches the whole line, not one column. If you search for 13 and you get more lines:

grep '13' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
grep '13' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
211

low_P   mock    ex61    55.3    13.3
low_P   mock    ex61    48.7    13.9
low_P   mock    ex64    46.93   13.52
In total this command gives us 36 extra lines, because 13 also appears in shoot weights such as 13.3. The first lines grep finds are not even 13C plants, but mock plants with such a shoot weight. In contrast, AWK compares only column 2, so this cannot happen making this a much safer command.

title: AWK on a table
text:
Keep rows by number
Comparisons also work with numbers: > (greater than), < (less than), >= and <= (greater or less than, or equal). To keep plants with roots longer than 50 mm:

awk -F'\t' '$4 > 50' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3
awk -F'\t' '$4 > 50' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    74.7    8.1
low_P   mock    ex61    66.5    8.9

476
Important: Note how the header is in the result? Column 4 of the header is the word Rootlength, not a number. When a value is not a number, AWK compares it as text, and in that comparison Rootlength counts as larger than 50. To avoid this we need to add NR > 1 to skip the header. To combine patterns we can use &&, which means “and”: both conditions must be true.

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 > 50' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
475
|| means “or”: We can use this if we want at least one of the conditions to be true.

# Low phosphorus and no bacteria
awk -F'\t' '$1 == "low_P" && $2 == "mock"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Either of the two bacteria
awk -F'\t' '$2 == "129E" || $2 == "13C"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt







QuestionExercise






How many plants grew with high phosphorus and bacterium 13C?
How many plants have a shoot weight above 20 mg?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# 1. Two text conditions with &&
awk -F'\t' '$1 == "high_P" && $2 == "13C"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

# 2. NR > 1 keeps the header out
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $5 > 20' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
87

140
So 87 plants grew with high phosphorus and 13C, and 140 plants have a shoot weight above 20 mg.

title: AWK on a table
text:
Missing values: empty fields
Now look for plants with very short roots, below 10 mm:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 < 10' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 < 10' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
15

high_P  mock    ex61        18.2
high_P  mock    ex64        22.4
high_P  mock    ex64        26
15 plants, but if we look at the table we notice that none of them has a root length below 10. Instead you will notice that these rows have no root length at all. If we use cat -A this will show us exactly what is in the file for these fields:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 < 10' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3 | cat -A

This prints:
high_P^Imock^Iex61^I^I18.2$
high_P^Imock^Iex64^I^I22.4$
high_P^Imock^Iex64^I^I26$
We see two tabs side by side, ^I^I, with nothing between them: this is an empty field and also how a missing value often looks, for example in a table saved from Excel with empty cells. Count them per column:

# Empty root length (column 4) and empty shoot weight (column 5)
awk -F'\t' '$4 == ""' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$5 == ""' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
15
8
Altogether, this tells us that AWK did not give an error but it did something we didn’t really want. It compared the empty field with 10 as text, and empty text counts as smaller than anything. So all 15 plants without a root length passed the filter $4 < 10. In calculations, AWK will treat an empty field as 0, as you see further down.






ImportantImportant: skip empty fields before you compare or calculate



Before you compare or calculate with a column, keep only the rows that have a value in it, with $4 != "". != means “is not equal to”, and "" is empty text, so $4 != "" means “column 4 is not empty”:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 != "" && $4 < 10' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
0
No plant in this table has roots shorter than 10 mm.



Why -F'\t' matters
AWK can also run without -F'\t'. It then splits lines at any run of spaces and tabs. For most lines in this table, the result is the same. But AWK then treats the two tabs around an empty field as one separator, and the values move one column to the left. Line 123 is the first row with an empty root length:

# Line 123, and its column 4 with -F'\t'
awk -F'\t' 'NR == 123' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt
awk -F'\t' 'NR == 123 { print $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Column 4 of the same line without -F'\t'
awk 'NR == 123 { print $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Number of fields per line without -F'\t'
awk '{ print NF }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
high_P  mock    ex61        18.2

18.2

     23 4
    572 5
With -F'\t', column 4 of line 123 is empty (the empty line in the output). Without it, column 4 is 18.2, the shoot weight. The 23 lines with an empty field now have only 4 fields. Again there is no error. The NF check from above shows the problem right away, so it is worth running on every new table.






QuestionExercise






How many plants have a shoot weight below 5 mg? First write the command without the rule from above. Then add the rule. What is the difference, and why?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Without the rule
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $5 < 5' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

# With the rule: skip empty shoot weights
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $5 != "" && $5 < 5' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
10
2
Only 2 plants have a shoot weight below 5 mg. The first command also keeps the 8 plants without a shoot weight.












TipTip: fill empty fields with NA (optional)





Empty fields are easy to miss. One way to make them visible is to fill each empty field with NA (not available) and save the result as a new file. In this table, only column 4 and column 5 have empty fields, so you fill those two:

# If column 4 is empty, put NA into it.
# If column 5 is empty, put NA into it.
# Then print every line.
# The command is spread over several lines to make it easier to read
# (more on this in "Add a column" below).
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  $4 == "" { $4 = "NA" }
  $5 == "" { $5 = "NA" }
  { print }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > Growth_Data_NA.txt

# Check: same number of lines, and line 123 now has NA
wc -l Growth_Data_NA.txt
awk -F'\t' 'NR == 123' Growth_Data_NA.txt

This prints:
595 Growth_Data_NA.txt
high_P  mock    ex61    NA  18.2
Also here -v OFS='\t' matters. When you change a field, AWK rebuilds the whole line and puts the output separator between the fields. Without -v OFS='\t', that is a space. Only the changed lines get spaces, the others keep their tabs, so the file now mixes both. cat -A shows this for line 123 (changed) and line 2 (not changed) of such a file:
high_P mock ex61 NA 18.2$
low_P^Imock^Iex61^I40.4^I6.6$
If you do not know which columns have empty fields, or there are many columns, you can let AWK go through all fields with a loop. You do not need to remember this form. Keep it in your notes, or ask an LLM for it and check the result as shown here. In this table it gives exactly the same file:

# For each field in the line (i = 1 up to the number of fields NF):
# if the field is empty, put NA into it. Then print the line.
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  {
    for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) {
      if ($i == "") { $i = "NA" }
    }
    print
  }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

Now the missing values are visible when you look at the file. Also, the columns no longer shift in tools that split at spaces and tabs, such as AWK without -F'\t', or join and column -t with their default settings.
But when you do this, it’s important to know that NA does not make comparisons safe. NA is text too, and in a text comparison it counts as larger than 50:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 > 50' Growth_Data_NA.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 != "NA" && $4 > 50' Growth_Data_NA.txt | wc -l

This prints:
490
475
So with NA, the rule stays the same, only with $4 != "NA" instead of $4 != "".

title: AWK on a table
text:
Add a column
AWK can calculate with fields. For example, the shoot weight per mm of root is $5 / $4. To add it as a new column at the end of each line, print the whole line $0 and then the result:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 { print $0, $5 / $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > shoot_per_root.txt

wc -l shoot_per_root.txt

This prints:
awk: cmd. line:1: (FILENAME=awk_data/Growth_Data.txt FNR=123) fatal: division by zero attempted
121 shoot_per_root.txt
The error message tells us that AWK stopped at line 123: the first row with an empty root length. That is because it treated the empty field as 0, and a division by 0 is not possible. The file shoot_per_root.txt still exists, but it has only 121 lines instead of 594. If you missed the error message and only looked at head, the file would look fine. This is why you want to make it a habit to count lines after each step.
To fix this, you need to skip rows with an empty root length or shoot weight, and print a header for the new column. The command now has two parts, each with its own pattern and action.
A command with several parts gets long on one line. AWK lets you spread the part between the single quotes over several lines, so you can put each pattern and its action on a line of its own. The command does exactly the same, it is only easier to read. You can copy it into your terminal as it is: the terminal waits for the closing quote before it runs the command.

# Part 1: on line 1, print the current header and add a name for the new column
# Part 2: on the other lines with both values, print the line plus the result
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  NR == 1                          { print $0, "shoot_per_root" }
  NR > 1 && $4 != "" && $5 != ""   { print $0, $5 / $4 }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > shoot_per_root.txt

# Check the result
head -3 shoot_per_root.txt
wc -l shoot_per_root.txt

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg shoot_per_root
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6 0.163366
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8 0.178947

572 shoot_per_root.txt
572 lines: the header plus 571 plants. Does that add up? 594 plants, minus 15 without a root length, minus 8 without a shoot weight, is 571. No plant misses both values, so no row is subtracted twice.






ImportantKeep the opening brace on the same line as its pattern



When you spread a command over several lines, the opening { of an action must stay on the same line as its pattern. If you move the { to the next line, AWK reads the pattern on its own (which prints every matching line) and the action on its own (which runs on every line). You get no error, only a different result.

title: AWK on a table
section: Sum and mean of a column: variables and END
text:
Sum and mean of a column: variables and END
You will notice that the commands from here on are longer than the ones before. You could do the same thing in R or Python, and you might wonder why even learn them in AWK? The reason is that in bioinformatics you often only need a quick look at your data: how many plants are in each group, and do the means look sensible? AWK gives you that answer in the terminal, without starting another program or loading the table first. On a computer cluster, where R or Python may not be set up for you, AWK is always there. And because AWK reads a file one line at a time, it also works on files that are too large to open comfortably in R or Excel. For statistics and plots, R or Python remain the better tools. AWK is for the quick check before, or for cleaning up a table before you load it there.
Start with one number: the total shoot weight of all plants. For this, AWK needs a variable, a named box that holds a value. You do not need to create it first: AWK makes the box the first time you use it, and it starts at 0.

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $5 != "" { sum += $5 } END { print sum }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
9715.23
Taken apart:

sum += $5: add the shoot weight of this line to the box sum. += means “add to what is already in the box”.
END { print sum }: END is a special pattern. Its action runs once, after AWK has read the last line. By then, sum holds the total.

The name sum is your own choice. You could call it total or weight instead, and get the same result. Names such as NR, NF and END are different: they belong to AWK and have a fixed meaning.
For the mean, you need a second box that counts the plants. Here it is called n (short for “number of plants”), and n++ adds 1 to it. The ; separates two steps inside one action:

awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 && $5 != "" { sum += $5; n++ }
  END                { print n, sum, sum / n }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints the number of plants, the total and the mean:
586 9715.23 16.5789
Does 586 add up? 594 plants, minus the 8 without a shoot weight, is 586.
Now leave out the rule for empty fields, and then also NR > 1:

# Without $5 != ""
awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 { sum += $5; n++ }
  END    { print n, sum, sum / n }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Also without NR > 1
awk -F'\t' '
  { sum += $5; n++ }
  END { print n, sum, sum / n }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
594 9715.23 16.3556

595 9715.23 16.3281
The total is the same all three times. AWK adds an empty field as 0, and the header text FW_shoot_mg as 0 too, so the sum does not change. But n still counts these lines, so the mean drops. A total that looks right does not mean that the mean is right. Look at the count as well: you expect 586.

title: AWK on a table
section: Count and mean per group: arrays
text:
Count and mean per group: arrays
sum and n are single boxes: each holds one value for the whole file. To count the plants per nutrient level, you need one box per group. A set of named boxes like this is called an array. n["low_P"] is the box for low_P, n["high_P"] the box for high_P. Just like a variable, AWK makes each box the first time you use it, and it starts at 0.

awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 { n[$1]++ }
  END    { for (group in n) { print group, n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
low_P 300

high_P 294
Taken apart:

NR > 1 { n[$1]++ }: for each row of data, add 1 to the box of its nutrient level. Piece by piece:

n is the name of the array, the set of boxes.
[$1] picks one box: the box named after the value in column 1. On a low_P row that is n["low_P"].
++ adds 1 to that box.

So after the first low_P row, n["low_P"] is 1, after the second it is 2, and so on.
END { ... }: as before, this runs once, after the last line.
for (group in n) { print group, n[group] }: go through all boxes in n. For each box, put its name into group, and print the name and the count.

You can check the result with tools from the CLI workshop:

cut -f1 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
      1 Nutrient
    294 high_P
    300 low_P
For a mean per group, you do the same as for the whole file, but with one sum box and one n box per group. sum[$1] += $4 adds the root length to the sum of its group.

# Without the rule for empty fields
awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 { sum[$1] += $4; n[$1]++ }
  END    { for (group in sum) { print group, n[group], sum[group] / n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# With the rule: skip empty root lengths
awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 && $4 != "" { sum[$1] += $4; n[$1]++ }
  END                { for (group in sum) { print group, n[group], sum[group] / n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
low_P 300 57.9494
high_P 294 88.9501

low_P 290 59.9477
high_P 289 90.489
Without the rule, AWK adds 0 for each empty root length and still counts the plant. Both means come out too low, and nothing warns you.

Mean per nutrient and condition
To group by two columns, glue them together into one box name: $1"-"$2 is column 1, a dash and column 2, for example low_P-mock. The dash goes in double quotes, because it is text here. A dash appears in none of the values, so you can split the name again later if you need to.

awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 && $4 != "" { group = $1"-"$2; sum[group] += $4; n[group]++ }
  END                { for (group in sum) { printf "%s\t%d\t%.1f\n", group, n[group], sum[group] / n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort

This prints:
high_P-129E 103 98.4
high_P-13C  85  97.7
high_P-mock 101 76.4
low_P-129E  99  69.9
low_P-13C   86  64.2
low_P-mock  105 47.1
Two new parts:

printf prints with a format that you choose. %s stands for text, %d for a whole number, %.1f for a number with one decimal, \t for a tab and \n for a new line. The values after the format fill these places in order.
| sort: AWK goes through the boxes in no fixed order. Sort the result, so that it is easy to read and to compare between runs.







ImportantForget the quotes, and the dash becomes a minus



If you write group = $1-$2 without the quotes, AWK reads the dash as a minus and subtracts column 2 from column 1. Text that does not start with a number counts as 0, so low_P and high_P both become 0, and 129E becomes 129. The command runs without an error, but prints this:
-129    202 84.4
-13 171 80.8
0   206 61.5
Three groups instead of six, and low_P and high_P plants mixed together. A quick check catches it: you expect 2 nutrient levels × 3 conditions = 6 groups, so count the lines of the output, and look at the group names.


Without the rule $4 != "", four of the six means are lower. For example, low_P with 129E gives 64.7 instead of 69.9, because the 8 plants without a root length count as 0 mm.






QuestionExercise






Calculate the mean shoot weight per Condition, with one decimal. How many plants are in each group?







AnswerClick me to see an answer





Condition is column 2, and the shoot weight is column 5. Skip the empty shoot weights:

awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 && $5 != "" { sum[$2] += $5; n[$2]++ }
  END                { for (group in sum) { printf "%s\t%d\t%.1f\n", group, n[group], sum[group] / n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort

This prints:
129E    208 17.6
13C 173 15.3
mock    205 16.6

title: AWK on a table
text:
What you learned

An AWK command has the shape awk -F'\t' 'pattern { action }' file.
$1, $2, … are the fields of a line, $0 the whole line, NF the number of fields, NR the line number.
Compare with ==, !=, >, <, and combine with && (and) and || (or). Text goes in double quotes.
A variable (sum += $5) and END give a total or a mean for the whole file; an array (sum[$1] += $5) gives one per group.
Look at the table first: cat -A for tabs and empty fields, NF for the number of fields per line.
Empty fields cause errors without a warning: skip them with $4 != "" before you compare or calculate.
After each step, check the result: count the lines, and look at it with head.

You do not need to learn these commands by heart. Instead, keep your own notes: a text file or notebook with the commands you have checked, each with one line on what it does and which trap it avoids (for example “skips empty fields in column 4”). A checked command in your notes is worth more than one you half remember, and more than a new one from an LLM that you still have to check.
On the next page, sed basics, you change text in a file: search and replace, delete lines, and clean up a file with Windows line endings.
